 Social Security changes coming in January 2027: 4 important things to know
 Published: Nov. 17, 2026, 6:00 a.m. 
 70 million people receive social security benefits, 56 million of whom are retirees and their dependents. (AP Photo/Nam Y. Huh, File) AP Photo/Nam Y. Huh 
 Set as Google Preferred Source 
 By Leada Gore | lgore@al.com 
 Tens of millions of Social Security and Supplemental Security Income recipients will see changes to their benefits starting in January 2027.
 Here are 4 changes you need to know:
 COLA increase
 Social Security and Supplemental Security Income (SSI) recipients will receive a 3.6% cost of living adjustment increase in 2027. SSI recipients will see the increase on Dec. 31, 2026; all other recipients will see it on their first payment of 2027.
 The average retiree receiving Social Security will see benefits increase about $75 a month, from an average of $2,095 to $2,170. More than 56 million retirees, dependents and disabled workers receive Social Security benefits and will see the increase.
 Average SSI benefits will increase:
 Individual - $1,029 per month, up $35 from 2026 
 Couples - $1,544 per month, up $53 from 2026 
 Essential persons - $516 a month, up $18 from 2026 
 More than 7 million people in the U.S. receive benefits through SSI. Payments average about $740 a month and go to low-income senior citizens, people with disabilities and people who are blind.
 Higher Maximum Taxable Earnings
 The Social Security Administration raised the maximum amount of earnings subject to the Social Security tax – known as Maximum Taxable Earnings or Contribution Base – from $184,500 to $192,300 in 2027. The change subjects more income to the payroll taxes that fund Social Security.
 Earnings above the $192,300 threshold are not subject to the Social Security tax, but Medicare’s 1.45% tax still applies, according to SSA.
 Social Security uses 35 highest-paid years to determine benefit amounts. However, only income up to the maximum taxable earnings limit is factored into that formula. That means if you earn more than the maximum taxable limit - the $192,300 figure in 2027 – the additional income won’t be taxed for Social Security but also won’t be used to increase your future benefits.
 Earnings limit change
 Social Security’s earnings limit caps how much beneficiaries can earn while collecting retirement benefits. Exceed that limit and monthly payments are reduced or withheld.
 The earnings limit for workers younger than full retirement age – 67 years old for anyone born 1960 or later – will increase to $25,560 in 2027. Social Security deducts $1 from benefits for every $2 earned over that amount.
 The earnings limit for people reaching their full retirement age in 2027 is increasing to $67,920. Social Security deducts $1 from benefits for every $3 earned over that amount until the month before the worker turns full retirement age.
 There is no limit on earnings for workers who are full retirement age or older for the entire year.
 Work credits increasing
 Workers will have to earn slightly more money in 2027 to receive credit towards qualifying for Social Security retirement benefits. 
 Social Security uses a work credit system to determine whether someone has been employed long enough to qualify for retirement benefits. Workers earn the credits based on how much money they make from their jobs and can earn a maximum of four credits per year. Benefits are calculated based on their highest 35 years of earnings and not credits, but you must have enough credits to qualify for your own Social Security benefits.
 Generally, a person needs 40 credits – roughly 10 years of employment - to qualify for Social Security.
 In 2026, each credit was $1,890 in earnings. In 2027, that amount increase to $1,970.
